724	399	### 4.8 Game-state awareness & control 🚧
725	400	
726	401	Note on numbering: this subsystem is logically a peer of §4.2–§4.6 (a video-frame consumer that emits typed events plus a controller that issues actuator commands). It lives at §4.8 only to avoid renumbering existing sections referenced from the journal and milestones.
727	402	
728	403	#### 4.8.1 Role
729	404	
730	405	Two related capabilities, both grounded in CV on the captured video stream:
731	406	
732	407	1. **Game-state observer.** Watch the screen; recognize what context the game is currently in — main menu, song-select, difficulty-select, in-game (gameplay), pause, score summary, etc. Surface that as typed events that the operator UI can render and the orchestrator below can act on.
733	408	2. **Game controller.** Expose high-level verbs ("start a single-player playthrough of song X on Hard", "go to the main menu", "select Practice mode"). Translate each verb into a sequence of fret/strum commands using the recognized current state and a known menu graph, monitor the screen for the expected state transitions, retry or back out on mismatch.
734	409	
735	410	This is *not* the gameplay note-detection path (§4.2). cv_marvin_v1 plays notes during gameplay; the game-state module decides *what to play* at the session level (which song, which difficulty, which mode) and gets us there from any starting screen.
736	411	
737	412	#### 4.8.2 Module shape
738	413	
739	414	- Owns its own FreeRTOS task (`game_task`).
740	415	- Subscribes to the video frame queue via the same multi-subscriber API used by detectors (§4.2.4); it is a video-frame consumer, **not** a detector. Its events do not flow on `xDetectorStateQueue`.
741	416	- Emits typed events on a separate, narrow bus (`xGameStateQueue`) — current_state changes, ambiguity warnings, error states.
742	417	- Orchestrator state for high-level verbs (current goal, expected next state, retry counter) lives inside `game_task`.
743	418	- Issues control commands by writing fret/strum bitmasks into the same fretboard-link path used by gameplay. Whether this routes through the timing pipeline (§4.4) or bypasses it is open Q11.
744	419	
745	420	#### 4.8.3 Game catalog & menu metadata
746	421	
747	422	The recognizer and the navigator both depend on per-game data:
748	423	
749	424	- **Recognizer templates.** Per-state visual signatures used by the CV recognizer — could be small reference images (template matching), color histograms, or text regions for OCR. Format chosen with the recognizer algorithm (open Q10).
750	425	- **Menu graph.** Nodes = recognized game states; edges = button sequences that move between them (e.g., "main_menu → song_select" = `[STRUM_DOWN, STRUM_DOWN, GREEN]`). Used by the navigator to plan a verb.
751	426	- **Song catalog.** Per-supported-game list of songs with the menu coordinates needed to select each one (which difficulty submenu, ordinal position in the list, etc.). Possibly augmented with metadata (BPM, length, expected difficulty score) for UI display and for reference-data labeling.
752	427	
753	428	Storage: compile-time tables for the per-game graph + a JSON or similar on the SD card for songlists and any user-editable bits. Exact split deferred until first concrete game is added.
754	429	
755	430	Scope today: target is **one game** — Guitar Hero (Wii) — to validate the design. Adding a second game is a metadata addition (new template set + new menu graph + new song catalog), not a structural change.
756	431	
757	432	#### 4.8.4 Interaction with other subsystems
758	433	
759	434	- **Detection (§4.2):** independent. cv_marvin_v1 runs only when the game-state observer reports `gameplay`. Outside gameplay, cv_marvin_v1 may be disabled to free CPU.
760	435	- **Timing pipeline (§4.4):** during gameplay the timing pipeline drives the actuators from detector-state. Outside gameplay it's idle, and the game-state controller drives actuators directly. Coordination and arbitration between the two is open Q11.
761	436	- **Operator UI (§4.5):** consumes game-state events to display the current screen the game is on; offers verbs as buttons / song-list pickers.
762	437	- **Recording (§4.6):** game-state transitions are useful session metadata. Either annotated into `state.bin` as a side channel or a sibling file (`game_state.bin`). To be decided when the recorder lands.
763	438	- **Fretboard link (§4.3):** shared command path. The fretboard MCU does not know whether a press is "gameplay note" or "menu navigation" — they're the same wire bits.
764	439	
765	440	#### 4.8.5 Open questions surfaced here
766	441	
767	442	See §9 for tracking entries. In summary:
768	443	
769	444	- **Q10** — Recognizer algorithm: template matching vs simple OCR vs region/color heuristics vs a small CNN. Trade-off is robustness vs CPU cost vs metadata authoring effort.
770	445	- **Q11** — Command-path arbitration between game-state controller and timing pipeline. Default is "they don't run at the same time" (gameplay vs menu), but the boundary needs to be explicit.
771	446	
772	447	### 4.9 Operator command console ✅
773	448	
774	449	An **interactive text console** over **FLEXCOM2 USART (115 200 8N1, ring-buffer mode)** — marvin's `PA13` (FLEXCOM2_IO0, `CLI_TX`) / `PA14` (FLEXCOM2_IO1, `CLI_RX`) — deliberately on a separate channel from the DBGU log/printf chatter — log output stays on DBGU, console I/O stays on FLEXCOM2, so neither pollutes the other.
775	450	
776	451	- **Why not Harmony `SYS_CONSOLE`/`SYS_COMMAND`:** those are MCC-config-coupled and live in regenerated files (this board already carries ~10 re-apply patches against clobbered generated code). The console is instead a small in-tree module (`console/console.{h,c}`) in the same shape as `fretboard_link`/`perf_log`: it owns the USART plib directly, is fully statically allocated, and is kept out of MCC via `user.cmake`.
777	452	- **Library:** [embedded-cli](https://github.com/funbiscuit/embedded-cli) (vendored under `default/src/third_party/embedded-cli/`, MIT), used in static-allocation mode (a fixed `CLI_UINT` buffer → no `malloc`). Provides line editing, history, and tab-completion.
778	453	- **Mechanics:** one FreeRTOS task drains the FLEXCOM2 RX ring (woken by a 1-byte read-threshold notification, like `fretboard_rx_task`), feeds bytes to embedded-cli, and runs the dispatcher. Output is written byte-by-byte into the TX ring.
779	454	- **Commands (v0):** `status`, `detect <cv|adc> <on|off>`, `active <cv|adc>`, `timing <on|off>`, `manual <on|off>`, `fret <g|r|y|b|o> <0|1>`, `strum <down|up>` — dispatching into the existing `Detector_*`, `TimingPipeline_SetEnabled`, and `ManualControl_*` setters. The binding table is a plain static array; adding a command is one row. Maps onto the §6 operating-mode toggles. (`record`/`game_*` toggles and runtime timing-constant setters are deferred until those subsystems / setters exist.)

867	# Wiimote Bluetooth Technology Summary
868	
869	## Bluetooth Technology Type
870	The Wiimote uses **Bluetooth Classic (BR/EDR)** with the standard **Bluetooth HID protocol**, not Bluetooth Low Energy. The device is built around a Broadcom BCM2042 Bluetooth System-on-a-Chip.
871	
872	## Device Identification
873	The SDP (Service Discovery Protocol) reports these details:
874	
875	| Property | Value |
876	|----------|-------|
877	| Device Name | Nintendo RVL-CNT-01 (original) or RVL-CNT-01-TR (newer) |
878	| Vendor ID | 0x057e |
879	| Product ID | 0x0306 (original) or 0x0330 (newer) |
880	
881	## Pairing & Connection Process
882	The connection sequence involves:
883	
884	1. **Discovery**: Press the Sync button to enter discoverable mode for 20 seconds; LEDs blink indicating battery level
885	2. **Authentication**: Host sends authentication request; Wiimote responds with PIN challenge
886	3. **PIN Exchange**: The PIN is the Bluetooth address in reverse binary format (bonding mode uses host address; temporary mode uses Wiimote address)
887	4. **Data Channel**: After authentication succeeds, establish HID connection on PSM 0x13 (data pipe) and 0x11 (control pipe)
888	
889	## HID Report Structure
890	Communication uses unidirectional reports identified by hexadecimal report IDs. "Input" reports flow from device to host (prepended with 0xa1); "Output" reports flow from host to device (prepended with 0xa2). Over 20 different report types support features like buttons, accelerometer, IR camera, rumble, and speaker control.
891	```

935	31	| 2026-06-11 | **NAND programming from macOS = u-boot RAM-loaded over JTAG, as a PMECC-aware flasher; the boot region needs a hand-prepended PMECC header.** New flow in [`openocd/program-nand.{sh,cfg,md}`](../openocd/program-nand.md): the init-and-stop at91bootstrap brings up DDR (as `load-ram`), then we `load_image` the at91bootstrap + `harmony.bin` + `u-boot.bin` into DDR and jump to u-boot; u-boot's `atmel_nand` (`nand erase`/`nand write`) burns NAND with PMECC. Built `u-boot.bin` from `sam9x75_curiosity_pro_nandflash_defconfig` (macOS: `gmake`, OpenSSL via the **environment** so dtc's bundled-libfdt include isn't clobbered). **Validated on hardware: marvin boots standalone from NAND** (RomBOOT → at91bootstrap copies `0x100000` from `0x40000` → marvin runs, HDMI captured). | Closes the 2026-06-09 "macOS-native NAND is Phase-2 R&D" item. OpenOCD's `at91sam9` NAND driver can't do PMECC, so it can't write a bootable boot region; u-boot's driver uses the same PMECC IP and its DT (hw ECC, **8-bit/512, eccOffset 152** = `oobsize − 8·13`) matches both the chip's ONFI (`nand info`: 4096/256/8/512) and the at91bootstrap header generator — so `nand write` is RomBOOT-correct. **Two non-obvious gotchas, both bench-found:** (1) The SAM9X7 ROM reads page 0 *without ECC* expecting a NAND header — 52 copies of a 32-bit word, code at offset `0xD0` (DS60001813D p.159/162). SAM-BA's `writeboot` synthesizes this; a plain `nand write` does not, so headerless writes give RomBOOT-only (no boot). Fix: prepend the header with `binaries/make-pmecchead.sh` (wraps at91bootstrap `addpmecchead.py`) using the **real** chip params → word `0xc2605007`; *not* that script's SAM9X7 defaults (2048/64/4), which don't match this board. (2) u-boot's default `bootcmd` reads the empty kernel partition into `0x22000000`/`0x21000000`; a 3 s autoboot overwrites staged blobs with `0xff` before you can program. Fix: stage into `0x21100000`/`0x21200000` (outside its read windows) and stop autoboot on connect. QSPI path still SAM-BA (no OpenOCD driver). |

The `CDC_WRITE_COMPLETE` perf-stage name is now historical (it's a UART enqueue) but kept to avoid a host-decoder schema change. |

The TPL/IAD match accepts the device (host stack does call `interfaceAssign`), but the per-interface check inside `F_USB_HOST_CDC_InterfaceAssign` then rejects the comm interface, the interrupt pipe never opens, the CDC instance flips to STATE_ERROR, and our attach handler never fires. Both are CDC ACM in practice and Linux/macOS accept either. Two-line OR per check in `usb_host_cdc.c`; logged as patch #7 in the re-apply list. |
1018	- **Single-screen attach assumption for `ui/manual_input`.** `screenHide_Screen0` deletes the root widget tree, taking the Composer-generated `Screen0_*` widget pointers with it. We bind callbacks once after the first `screenShow_Screen0`. If a second Legato screen is ever added, `ManualInput_Bind` must re-run inside that screen's show path (or whichever screen owns the manual-control widgets). Not an issue today — flagged for whenever the operator UI grows beyond Screen0.
1019	- **Result:** macOS 26 (Tahoe) still shows **4** ports (`/dev/cu.usbserial-W16_2026_3590..3`) — `AppleUSBFTDI` does not consult the per-channel VCP flag. Port-hiding is not achievable on macOS this way; kept the flash for the identity/serial benefit (see decision log). JTAG re-verified working post-flash (halt at pc≈0x0030dc40).
1020	**Multi-IRP pipelining via UDPHS driver patch.** The journal's "lever 1" hypothesis (pipeline CDC writes for 2-3× win) had a hidden gotcha. The CDC layer accepts multiple in-flight IRPs (`queueSizeWrite` and `USB_DEVICE_CDC_QUEUE_DEPTH_COMBINED` are both knobs), but the underlying UDPHS device driver only programs the DMA channel in `IRPSubmit`'s queue-empty branch. Subsequent IRPs are linked into the endpoint's queue but *never armed for transmission* — `Tasks_ISR_DMA` advances `irpQueue = irp->next` after a callback fires but doesn't re-program the DMA hardware. Net effect: even with all three layers configured for N=3 in-flight, only one IRP ever transmitted; the other two sat as `STATUS_PENDING` in the linked list forever.
1021	**Class-driver binding.** Enumeration succeeded but the CDC attach handler never fired. Added per-interface descriptor logging inside `F_USB_HOST_UpdateDeviceTask` to see what was actually being matched. Output revealed VID `0x03EB` PID `0x2175` — an EDBG composite with five interfaces: HID/CMSIS-DAP, CDC ACM IAD pair (comm + data), vendor, MSC. The IAD passed TPL match and got assigned to the CDC driver, but the CDC instance still flipped to `STATE_ERROR` without our app-level handler ever seeing the attach.

# Guitar Hero Wii Guitar Controller Overview

## Extension Identifier
The guitar is identified by six bytes at register 0x(4)a400fa: `00 00 A4 20 01 03`. The first byte being `00` indicates a guitar (versus `01` for drums).

## Initialization Sequence
For Guitar Hero 3 Gibson Les Paul guitars, the old initialization method works directly. However, for GHWT and third-party guitars, you must:
1. Write `0x55` to register `0x(4)a400f0`
2. Write `0` to register `0x(4)a400fb`

This enables reading the identification bytes and disables encryption on all expansion data.

## Data Report Format (6 bytes)

| **Byte** | **Contents** |
|----------|------------|
| 0 | GH3 flags (bits 7-6); Analog stick X (bits 5-0) |
| 1 | GH3 flags (bits 7-6); Analog stick Y (bits 5-0) |
| 2 | Touch bar value (bits 3-0) |
| 3 | Whammy bar (bits 3-0) |
| 4 | Fret buttons: Green, Red, Yellow, Blue, Orange (bits 6,4,2,0); Plus/Minus buttons (bits 5,3); reserved (bits 7,1) |
| 5 | Orange fret, Red fret, Blue fret, Green fret, Yellow fret, effects pedal, reserved, Strum up/down (bits 7-0) |
```

The original ESP32 has a Classic BT radio — an S3/C3 would *not* have worked.
- **This is new** — no prior discussion in the repo; today's specstory is the first mention.
- **It's an architectural pivot.** Marvin's current design has the **fretboard** physically pressing buttons on a *real* Wii guitar controller via open-drain GPIO. A Wiimote-emulating ESP32 would instead *be* the controller — receiving commands from Marvin and speaking Bluetooth HID straight to the Wii, taking the physical actuator + real controller out of the loop.
- **Important nuance:** a Wii guitar isn't a Wiimote — it's an *extension* read over the Wiimote's I²C extension bus. So the ESP32 must emulate a **Wiimote that reports an attached Guitar Hero guitar extension** (I have the extension ID `00 00 A4 20 01 03` and the 6-byte report layout for frets/strum/whammy/touchbar).
- **Risk note:** device-side Wiimote *emulation* (vs. host-side, which is common) is rare. The ESP-IDF BT-Classic HID-device stack uses the same PSMs the Wiimote uses, and the SDP record is customizable, so it's feasible — but matching the descriptor, VID/PID, device class, and the Wii's pairing flow (PIN = reversed BD_ADDR) is the hard part. I'd want a feasibility spike before committing.

# Plan: ESP32 Wiimote (+ guitar extension) emulator — new subproject

## Context

Marvin's current design closes the loop by having the **fretboard** MCU physically
press buttons on a *real* Wii guitar controller via open-drain GPIO. This plan
explores an alternative: an **Adafruit ESP32 Feather V2 (product 5400)** that
*emulates* a Wiimote with an attached Guitar Hero guitar extension, speaking
Bluetooth straight to the Wii. Marvin would eventually drive it with high-level
fret/strum commands, removing the physical actuator + real controller from the loop.

Per the decision this session, we build this as a **parallel, independent
proof-of-concept** — the existing fretboard path stays intact and authoritative
until this is proven. We de-risk the hard/novel part (device-side Bluetooth
emulation) before touching Marvin. The **Marvin↔ESP32 link is deferred**; early
phases use a local test driver.

### Key technical facts (verified)
- **Board:** Adafruit 5400 = ESP32 Feather V2 — *original* dual-core ESP32, which has
  a **Bluetooth Classic (BR/EDR)** radio. (S3/C3 are BLE-only and would not work.)
- **Wiimote transport:** Bluetooth Classic **HID** over L2CAP — PSM `0x11` (control),
  PSM `0x13` (data). Input reports prefixed `0xa1`, output reports `0xa2`.
- **Identity the Wii expects (SDP):** device name `Nintendo RVL-CNT-01`,
  VID `0x057e`, PID `0x0306`, plus a matching Class-of-Device and HID descriptor.
- **Pairing PIN:** legacy PIN = the device's own BD_ADDR in **reverse byte order**
  (raw 6 bytes) for the "press 1+2" temporary-pair flow. We know our own address, so
  we can supply it via the GAP PIN-request callback.
- **Guitar extension:** ID bytes `00 00 A4 20 01 03` at register `0x(4)a400fa`;
  init = write `0x55`→`0xf0`, `0x00`→`0xfb` (disables encryption). 6-byte report:
  frets (G/R/Y/B/O), strum up/down, whammy (byte 3, bits 3-0), touch bar, stick,
  +/− buttons. Reported inside a Wiimote data report that includes extension bytes
  (e.g. `0x34` = core buttons + 19 extension bytes).
- **Risk:** host-side Wiimote use is common; *device-side emulation to a real Wii is
  rare*. The ESP-IDF BT-Classic HID-device stack uses the same PSMs, and SDP is
  customizable, so it's feasible — but matching the SDP/descriptor/CoD and the Wii's
  pairing+polling flow is the crux. Phases 1–2 exist specifically to retire that risk
  before any guitar or Marvin work.

## Subproject layout

New top-level firmware subproject: `firmware/wiimote-esp32/` (name adjustable).

\```
firmware/wiimote-esp32/
  SPEC.md            # what this is, interfaces, success criteria
  docs/journal.md    # planning/decisions/session log (repo convention)
  main/              # ESP-IDF app component
    main.c
    bt_hid_device.c  # Bluedroid BT-Classic HID device + SDP/CoD setup
    wiimote.c        # report state machine (output-report handling, input reports)
    extension.c      # guitar-extension register map + 6-byte report builder
    cmd_source.c     # test command driver (serial console / canned patterns)
  CMakeLists.txt
  sdkconfig.defaults # enable Classic BT + Bluedroid HID device, disable BLE
\```

Follow repo conventions: create `docs/journal.md` using the same structure as
`firmware/marvin/docs/journal.md`, add it to the journal list in `CLAUDE.md`, and
add a pointer row in the root `SPEC.md`. Application code follows the project's
**static-allocation** preference (no `malloc` in our code; Bluedroid's internal
allocation is framework-owned and out of scope).

## Phased implementation

**Phase 0 — Toolchain & board bring-up**
- Install/pin ESP-IDF (v5.x). Build + flash a blink/USB-serial-log sanity app to the
  Feather V2. Confirm the Classic BT radio initializes and the device is discoverable
  by name from a PC (`bluetoothctl`/phone) — proves the radio + Bluedroid path.

**Phase 1 — Bluetooth identity / pairing spike (highest risk; do first)**
- Bring up Bluedroid BT-Classic HID device (`esp_hidd_api.h`:
  `esp_bt_hid_device_register_app`, connect/report callbacks).
- Set Class-of-Device to the Wiimote value and publish an SDP record matching
  name `Nintendo RVL-CNT-01` / VID `0x057e` / PID `0x0306` with the Wiimote HID
  report descriptor (lifted from wiibrew / a real unit).
- Set BD_ADDR and implement the GAP PIN-request callback returning BD_ADDR-reversed.
- **Success:** a real Wii (sync/"press 1+2" flow) authenticates and opens the HID
  data channel on PSM 0x13 without immediately dropping. If `esp_hidd` forces an
  incompatible SDP, fall back to raw L2CAP on PSM 0x11/0x13 with a hand-built SDP
  record (note this fork in the journal).

**Phase 2 — Core Wiimote emulation**
- Handle host output reports: data-reporting-mode (`0x12`), status request (`0x15`),
  LED (`0x11`), rumble bit, read/write register (`0x16`/`0x17`).
- Send input reports: status (`0x20`) and core-buttons mode (`0x30`).
- **Success:** the Wii shows one stable connected Wiimote; button presses (from the
  test driver) move/click the Home-menu hand cursor and the connection survives.

**Phase 3 — Guitar extension emulation**
- Implement the extension register map: identity `00 00 A4 20 01 03` at `0xfa`,
  init writes (`0x55`→`0xf0`, `0`→`0xfb`), report extension-attached in status.

## Approved Plan (edited by user):
# Plan: ESP32 Wiimote (+ guitar extension) emulator — new subproject

## Context

Marvin's current design closes the loop by having the **fretboard** MCU physically
press buttons on a *real* Wii guitar controller via open-drain GPIO. This plan
explores an alternative: an **Adafruit ESP32 Feather V2 (product 5400)** that
*emulates* a Wiimote with an attached Guitar Hero guitar extension, speaking
Bluetooth straight to the Wii. Marvin would eventually drive it with high-level
fret/strum commands, removing the physical actuator + real controller from the loop.

Per the decision this session, we build this as a **parallel, independent
proof-of-concept** — the existing fretboard path stays intact and authoritative
until this is proven. We de-risk the hard/novel part (device-side Bluetooth
emulation) before touching Marvin. The **Marvin↔ESP32 link is deferred**; early
phases use a local test driver.

### Key technical facts (verified)
- **Board:** Adafruit 5400 = ESP32 Feather V2 — *original* dual-core ESP32, which has
  a **Bluetooth Classic (BR/EDR)** radio. (S3/C3 are BLE-only and would not work.)
- **Wiimote transport:** Bluetooth Classic **HID** over L2CAP — PSM `0x11` (control),
  PSM `0x13` (data). Input reports prefixed `0xa1`, output reports `0xa2`.
- **Identity the Wii expects (SDP):** device name `Nintendo RVL-CNT-01`,
  VID `0x057e`, PID `0x0306`, plus a matching Class-of-Device and HID descriptor.
- **Pairing PIN:** legacy PIN = the device's own BD_ADDR in **reverse byte order**
  (raw 6 bytes) for the "press 1+2" temporary-pair flow. We know our own address, so
  we can supply it via the GAP PIN-request callback.
- **Guitar extension:** ID bytes `00 00 A4 20 01 03` at register `0x(4)a400fa`;
  init = write `0x55`→`0xf0`, `0x00`→`0xfb` (disables encryption). 6-byte report:
  frets (G/R/Y/B/O), strum up/down, whammy (byte 3, bits 3-0), touch bar, stick,
  +/− buttons. Reported inside a Wiimote data report that includes extension bytes
  (e.g. `0x34` = core buttons + 19 extension bytes).
- **Risk:** host-side Wiimote use is common; *device-side emulation to a real Wii is
  rare*. The ESP-IDF BT-Classic HID-device stack uses the same PSMs, and SDP is
  customizable, so it's feasible — but matching the SDP/descriptor/CoD and the Wii's
  pairing+polling flow is the crux. Phases 1–2 exist specifically to retire that risk
  before any guitar or Marvin work.

## Subproject layout

New top-level firmware subproject: `firmware/fauxmote/`.

```
firmware/fauxmote/
  SPEC.md            # what this is, interfaces, success criteria
  docs/journal.md    # planning/decisions/session log (repo convention)
  main/              # ESP-IDF app component
    main.c
    bt_hid_device.c  # Bluedroid BT-Classic HID device + SDP/CoD setup
    wiimote.c        # report state machine (output-report handling, input reports)
    extension.c      # guitar-extension register map + 6-byte report builder
    cmd_source.c     # test command driver (serial console / canned patterns)
  CMakeLists.txt
  sdkconfig.defaults # enable Classic BT + Bluedroid HID device, disable BLE
```

Follow repo conventions: create `docs/journal.md` using the same structure as
`firmware/marvin/docs/journal.md`, add it to the journal list in `CLAUDE.md`, and
add a pointer row in the root `SPEC.md`. Application code follows the project's
**static-allocation** preference (no `malloc` in our code; Bluedroid's internal
allocation is framework-owned and out of scope).

## Phased implementation

**Phase 0 — Toolchain & board bring-up**
- Install/pin ESP-IDF (v5.x). Build + flash a blink/USB-serial-log sanity app to the
  Feather V2. Confirm the Classic BT radio initializes and the device is discoverable
  by name from a PC (`bluetoothctl`/phone) — proves the radio + Bluedroid path.

**Phase 1 — Bluetooth identity / pairing spike (highest risk; do first)**
- Bring up Bluedroid BT-Classic HID device (`esp_hidd_api.h`:
  `esp_bt_hid_device_register_app`, connect/report callbacks).
- Set Class-of-Device to the Wiimote value and publish an SDP record matching
  name `Nintendo RVL-CNT-01` / VID `0x057e` / PID `0x0306` with the Wiimote HID
  report descriptor (lifted from wiibrew / a real unit).
- Set BD_ADDR and implement the GAP PIN-request callback returning BD_ADDR-reversed.
- **Success:** a real Wii (sync/"press 1+2" flow) authenticates and opens the HID
  data channel on PSM 0x13 without immediately dropping. If `esp_hidd` forces an
  incompatible SDP, fall back to raw L2CAP on PSM 0x11/0x13 with a hand-built SDP
  record (note this fork in the journal).

**Phase 2 — Core Wiimote emulation**
- Handle host output reports: data-reporting-mode (`0x12`), status request (`0x15`),
  LED (`0x11`), rumble bit, read/write register (`0x16`/`0x17`).
- Send input reports: status (`0x20`) and core-buttons mode (`0x30`).
- **Success:** the Wii shows one stable connected Wiimote; button presses (from the
  test driver) move/click the Home-menu hand cursor and the connection survives.

**Phase 3 — Guitar extension emulation**
- Implement the extension register map: identity `00 00 A4 20 01 03` at `0xfa`,
  init writes (`0x55`→`0xf0`, `0`→`0xfb`), report extension-attached in status.
- Build the 6-byte guitar report and embed it in a data report carrying extension
  bytes (e.g. `0x34`). Encode frets/strum/whammy from the test driver.
- **Success:** a real Guitar Hero / Rock Band Wii title detects the guitar and
  responds to scripted notes in-game.

**Phase 4 — Command source (Marvin link still deferred)**
- Keep a local `cmd_source` driver (serial console + canned chord/strum patterns) so
  the emulator is independently testable. Document a clean seam where Marvin's
  command stream will later attach (likely the existing fretboard 1-byte fret/strum
  bitmask over UART — to be decided in a later session).

## Critical files / references to reuse
- Journal/spec **structure**: `firmware/marvin/docs/journal.md`, `firmware/marvin/docs/spec.md`,
  `firmware/fretboard/SPEC.md`.
- Future command protocol to mirror: the fretboard 1-byte fret/strum bitmask
  (`firmware/fretboard/SPEC.md`, button-output section) — for Phase 4+ only.
- ESP-IDF reference example: `bluetooth/esp_hid_device` (BT-Classic HID device).
- Protocol references: wiibrew `Wiimote` and `Guitar Hero (Wii) Guitars` pages.

## Verification
- **Phase 0:** device shows up by name in a PC/phone Bluetooth scan; serial log boots.
- **Phase 1:** Wii pairing/sync completes; HID data channel opens and stays up
  (confirm via ESP32 serial log of L2CAP connect + first poll).
- **Phase 2:** real Wii Home menu — emulated buttons drive the cursor; connection
  stable for minutes.
- **Phase 3:** real Guitar Hero/Rock Band Wii game detects the guitar; scripted
  fret+strum patterns register as hits in-game.
- Hardware needed: Wii console, a Wii guitar-game disc, USB-C cable for flashing/logs.
  (No automated test harness — this is hardware-in-the-loop validation.)

## Out of scope (this plan)
- Retiring or modifying the fretboard GPIO-press path (fretboard stays authoritative).
- The concrete Marvin↔ESP32 wiring/protocol (deferred by decision).
- Any edge-ai retargeting toward the emulator.
```

Aligned-pointer slot reads/writes are atomic on Cortex-A5 so the IRQ can scan without locking; `taskENTER_CRITICAL` only needed in `Subscribe`/`Unsubscribe` to prevent two task-side writers racing on the same empty slot. Nocache is simpler and bug-resistant — every reader sees DMA-fresh bytes without explicit maintenance. 1	# Guitar Hero Bot — System Specification
2	
3	> Top-level overview. For implementation detail of any single subproject, follow the pointers in §3. Each subproject owns its own spec; this document does not duplicate them.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## 1. Mission
8	
9	Build an autonomous robot that plays Guitar Hero / Rock Band on a real Wii guitar controller by watching the game video, detecting notes in real time, and pressing physical buttons in sync with the music. The system must run end-to-end without a host PC in the runtime path, produce reference-quality detector output that lighter detectors can be trained against, and provide an on-device operator UI for calibration, mode control, and replay.
10	
11	## 2. Current architecture
12	
13	Three pieces, one runtime brain:
14	
15	```
16	Wii ──HDMI──► ElectronWarp ──HDMI──► TC358743 ──CSI-2──┐
17	                                                       ▼
18	   ┌──────────────────────  marvin (SAM9X75)  ────────────┐
19	   │  HDMI capture → CV detect → timing pipeline → cmds   │
20	   │           ↑              detector-state bus          │
21	   │           │                       ▲                  │
22	   │           │  10.1″ LVDS + maxtouch │                  │
23	   │           │       (operator UI)    │                  │
24	   │           └────────── SD card ─────┘  (recording)    │
25	   └────────┬──────────────────────────┬───────────────────┘
26	            │ FLEXCOM2 UART (cmds)     │ FLEXCOM2 UART (ADC)
27	            ▼                          │
28	   ┌──────────────────────────────────┐│
29	   │   fretboard (PIC32CM6408)        │┘
30	   │   ADC scan ↔ open-drain GPIO     │
31	   └────────┬─────────────────────────┘
32	            │ GPIO
33	            ▼
34	   Wii guitar controller ──► Wii (closes the loop)
35	
36	                ◇ off-band: dev PC running fret-tuner
37	                  (calibration / detector tuning / replay)
38	```
39	
40	**Per-tier role summary:**
41	
42	- **marvin** — SAM9X75 Curiosity host. Owns HDMI capture, the *reference* CV note detector, ingest of fretboard ADC samples, the chord/strum timing pipeline, command emission to fretboard, the on-device LVDS+touch operator UI, and reference-data recording to SD. The runtime brain.
43	- **fretboard** — PIC32CM6408PL10048 MCU on a sensor/actuator board. Streams 5-channel phototransistor ADC up to marvin and converts incoming bitmask commands into open-drain GPIO presses on a Wii guitar controller. Has a standalone fallback mode where it runs its own chord FIFO without marvin in the loop.
44	- **fret-tuner** — Off-band Python tool (FastAPI + browser UI, Linux/macOS PC). Used at the bench for sensor calibration, detector-algorithm tuning, and replay analysis of recordings produced by marvin. Not in the runtime path.
45

90	| PIC32CM6408PL10048 | fretboard MCU | [fretboard spec](firmware/fretboard/SPEC.md) |
91	| LAN8651B1 (10BASE-T1S MAC-PHY) | *planned* fretboard ↔ marvin link over single-pair Ethernet + PoDL | [T1S/PoDL link](docs/t1s-podl-link.md) |
92	| Actuator mechanism (TBD: voice coil / electromagnet / DIY solenoid) | physical fret + strum drive | [`hardware/actuators/`](hardware/actuators/) and [`hardware/3d-models/`](hardware/3d-models/) |
93	| ElectronWarp | component → HDMI converter for Wii | external commercial part |
94	
95	The actuator choice is intentionally still open — `hardware/actuators/` contains design + test-protocol docs for three candidates.
96	
97	## 6. Cross-cutting decisions
98	
99	- **Architecture pivot.** The original PC-hosted / Elgato-USB-capture / PS2 / single-PIC-actuator design is retired. Source documents are preserved at [`docs/archive/`](docs/archive/) for design-rationale reference; they are *not* maintained.
100	- **`frame_epoch` is the master sync token.** A 32-bit counter incremented by marvin's video task on every captured ISC frame. Every detector-state record, emitted command, and recording artifact — including data from off-board observers — keys off this token so multi-source data can be aligned post-hoc. Detail in [marvin spec §4.6](firmware/marvin/docs/spec.md).
101	- **Reference data persists on marvin's SD card.** Detector-state + sparse raw BGR888 keyframes (default 1 keyframe/sec) + raw ADC stream + emitted commands. Off-board detectors record their own data keyed by `frame_epoch` and align offline.
102	- **Centralized timing on marvin, with a fretboard-takeover fallback.** marvin runs the chord-window FIFO and strum scheduler by default; an operator-mode toggle hands timing back to fretboard's standalone `fret_button.c` while marvin still records observations.
103	- **Operating modes are independent toggles**, not a global state machine: `detect_enable`, `marvin_timing_enable`, `actuate_enable`, `record_enable`. Named modes (idle / calibrate / dry-run / play / replay / record) are presets over them.
104	- **Planned: fretboard ↔ marvin link moves to 10BASE-T1S + dumb PoDL.** Replace the FLEXCOM2/SERCOM UART pair with single-pair Ethernet via a LAN8651B1 MAC-PHY on each end. Motivation, in order: PoDL carries power *and* data on one pair to the guitar; better noise/cable tolerance; PLCA multidrop headroom; and demonstrating 10BASE-T1S + PoDL inside a larger Microchip system (SAM9X7 + LAN8651 + PIC32CM). Bandwidth is not a driver — the existing UART has ~12× headroom. PoDL is **dumb** (fixed voltage, no SCCP negotiation) and transparent to both MCUs. No IP stack — the host implements only SPI + the OPEN Alliance TC6 chunk protocol + minimal L2 framing, with the existing frame formats riding unchanged inside the Ethernet payload. Fits comfortably on the PIC32CM (est. ~6–10 KB flash / ~1–2 KB SRAM); marvin is bare-metal so it gets a shared portable `oa_tc6` driver, not a free netdev. Detail in [`docs/t1s-podl-link.md`](docs/t1s-podl-link.md).
105

127

129	
130	- **Not PC-hosted.** marvin is the runtime brain; no host PC is required for play.
131	- **Not USB-capture / Elgato.** Video is captured directly off HDMI via a TC358743 → MIPI CSI-2 path into the SAM9X75's ISC.
132	- **Not PS2.** The supported console is the Nintendo Wii (with an ElectronWarp component → HDMI converter).
133	- **Not a single-MCU actuator.** Sensing and timing live on marvin; fretboard is a sensor/actuator MCU, not a solo controller (with the explicit exception of the standalone-fallback mode).
134	- **Not OpenCV / Python at runtime.** CV runs natively on the SAM9X75 (Cortex-A5). Python (`fret-tuner`) is a bench tool only.

# fauxmote — Specification

> What fauxmote *is* (purpose, hardware, interfaces, success criteria, milestones).
> The running diary of decisions and progress lives in [`docs/journal.md`](docs/journal.md) — read it alongside this on any non-trivial task.

## 1. Purpose

fauxmote is an **ESP32 firmware that emulates a Nintendo Wiimote with an attached
Guitar Hero guitar extension**, speaking Bluetooth straight to a real Wii console.
It is a **parallel proof-of-concept** alternative to the existing actuation path:
today the [fretboard](../fretboard/SPEC.md) MCU physically presses buttons on a
*real* Wii guitar controller via open-drain GPIO. fauxmote instead *becomes* the
controller — eventually driven by [marvin](../marvin/docs/spec.md)'s high-level
fret/strum commands, removing the physical actuator + real controller from the loop.

The fretboard GPIO-press path stays authoritative until fauxmote is proven; nothing
in marvin/fretboard/edge-ai changes as part of this subproject.

## 2. Hardware

| Component | Detail |
|---|---|
| Board | **Adafruit ESP32 Feather V2** (product 5400) — *original* dual-core ESP32 (Tensilica LX6), 8 MB flash, 2 MB PSRAM, USB-C. |
| Radio | ESP32 has a **Bluetooth Classic (BR/EDR)** radio — required, because the Wiimote link is Classic HID. (ESP32-S3/C3 are BLE-only and would *not* work.) |
| Wii console | Real retail Wii; pairing via the sync button or the controller's 1+2 button. |

## 3. The link fauxmote emulates (verified protocol facts)

- **Transport:** Bluetooth Classic **HID** over L2CAP — PSM `0x11` (control),
  PSM `0x13` (data). Input reports (device→host) prefixed `0xa1`; output reports
  (host→device) prefixed `0xa2`.
- **Identity the Wii expects (SDP):** device name `Nintendo RVL-CNT-01`,
  VID `0x057e`, PID `0x0306`, matching Class-of-Device, and the Wiimote HID report
  descriptor.
- **Pairing PIN (legacy):** the PIN is a BD_ADDR in **reverse byte order** (raw 6
  bytes). The 1+2 temporary-pair flow uses the *Wiimote's own* address — which
  fauxmote knows — so fauxmote can answer the GAP PIN request itself.
- **Guitar extension:** identity bytes `00 00 A4 20 01 03` at register
  `0x(4)a400fa`; init = write `0x55`→`0xf0`, `0x00`→`0xfb` (disables encryption).
  6-byte report layout (frets G/R/Y/B/O, strum up/down, whammy in byte 3 bits 3-0,
  touch bar, analog stick, +/− buttons), carried inside a Wiimote data report that
  includes extension bytes (e.g. report `0x34`).

References: wiibrew [`Wiimote`](https://wiibrew.org/wiki/Wiimote) and
[`Guitar Hero (Wii) Guitars`](https://wiibrew.org/wiki/Wiimote/Extension_Controllers/Guitar_Hero_(Wii)_Guitars).

## 4. Interfaces

- **Downstream (fauxmote → Wii):** Bluetooth Classic HID, as above.
- **Upstream (commands → fauxmote):** **deferred.** Early phases use a local test
  command source (serial console + canned chord/strum patterns). The eventual marvin
  link is undecided; the likely candidate is mirroring the fretboard 1-byte fret/strum
  bitmask over UART (see [fretboard SPEC](../fretboard/SPEC.md) button-output section).
- **Debug:** USB-C CDC serial for flashing + logs (`idf.py monitor`).

## 5. Software

- **Framework:** ESP-IDF (v5.x), Bluedroid stack in **Bluetooth-Classic-only** mode
  (BLE disabled). Bluedroid's BT-Classic HID-device API (`esp_hidd_api.h`) is the
  starting point; raw L2CAP on PSM 0x11/0x13 with a hand-built SDP record is the
  fallback if the stack's default SDP is too rigid for the Wii.
- **Allocation:** application code follows the project's **static-allocation**
  preference (no `malloc` in our code). Bluedroid's internal allocation is
  framework-owned and out of scope.

## 6. Milestones / success criteria

| Phase | Goal | Done when |
|---|---|---|
| **0** | Toolchain + radio bring-up | Builds + flashes to the Feather V2; the board is discoverable by name in a PC/phone Bluetooth scan. |
| **1** | Bluetooth identity / pairing (highest risk) | A real Wii authenticates and opens the HID data channel on PSM 0x13 without immediately dropping. |
| **2** | Core Wiimote emulation | Wii shows one stable connected Wiimote; emulated buttons drive the Home-menu cursor; connection survives minutes. |
| **3** | Guitar extension emulation | A real Guitar Hero / Rock Band Wii title detects the guitar and registers scripted fret+strum notes. |
| **4** | Command source | Local test driver (serial console + canned patterns) exercises the emulator independently; a clean seam is left for the future marvin link. |

## 7. Out of scope

- Retiring or modifying the fretboard GPIO-press path.
- The concrete marvin↔fauxmote wiring/protocol (deferred).
- Any edge-ai retargeting toward fauxmote.

# fauxmote — Working Journal

Running log of planning, decisions, open questions, and work-in-progress for fauxmote. Newest entries at the top. For *what fauxmote is* (purpose, hardware, interfaces, milestones), read [`../SPEC.md`](../SPEC.md) — this journal does not duplicate it.

---

## Current focus

**Phase 0 — toolchain + radio bring-up.** ESP-IDF project scaffold is in place
(`main/main.c` brings the Bluetooth-Classic radio up and advertises the board as
`Nintendo RVL-CNT-01`, discoverable). **Untested** — no toolchain/hardware run yet.
Next: install/pin ESP-IDF v5.x, `idf.py build flash monitor` on the Feather V2, and
confirm the board appears by name in a PC/phone Bluetooth scan.

Phase progression and success criteria are in [`../SPEC.md`](../SPEC.md) §6.

---

## Decision log

| Date | Decision | Rationale |
|------|----------|-----------|
| 2026-06-12 | **Build fauxmote as a parallel, independent proof-of-concept subproject; the fretboard GPIO-press path stays authoritative.** New top-level firmware subproject `firmware/fauxmote/`. | Device-side Wiimote *emulation* to a real Wii is rare/novel (host-side use is common), so de-risk it in isolation before touching marvin/fretboard/edge-ai. Nothing in the existing actuation path changes until fauxmote is proven. |
| 2026-06-12 | **Framework = ESP-IDF (v5.x), Bluedroid in Bluetooth-Classic-only mode (BLE disabled).** | Wiimote uses Bluetooth Classic HID; ESP-IDF exposes the BT-Classic HID-device API (`esp_hidd_api.h`), custom SDP records, BD_ADDR control, and raw L2CAP — all of which emulation needs. Arduino-ESP32's BT-Classic HID-device support is too thin for the custom SDP/descriptor the Wiimote requires. |
| 2026-06-12 | **Board = Adafruit ESP32 Feather V2 (product 5400); its *original* ESP32 is the load-bearing choice.** | The original ESP32 has a Bluetooth Classic (BR/EDR) radio. ESP32-S3/C3 are BLE-only and cannot emulate a Wiimote. Confirmed the product 5400 is the Feather V2 (not a QT Py S3). |
| 2026-06-12 | **marvin↔fauxmote command link is deferred; early phases use a local test command source.** | Lets the hard part (ESP32↔Wii Bluetooth emulation) be developed and validated standalone. The likely eventual link mirrors the fretboard 1-byte fret/strum bitmask over UART, but that's a later-session decision. |

---

## Open questions

- **Q1 — Does ESP-IDF's `esp_hidd` BT-Classic HID device let us publish the exact SDP record the Wii expects** (name `Nintendo RVL-CNT-01`, VID `0x057e`, PID `0x0306`, Wiimote HID descriptor, matching Class-of-Device)? If its default SDP is too rigid, fall back to raw L2CAP on PSM 0x11/0x13 with a hand-built SDP record. Resolve in Phase 1.
- **Q2 — Which pairing flow to target first?** The 1+2 temporary-pair flow uses the Wiimote's *own* BD_ADDR (reversed) as the PIN, which fauxmote knows and can answer in the GAP PIN-request callback. The sync-button permanent flow uses the *host (Wii)* address. Start with 1+2.
- **Q3 — Exact Class-of-Device value** the Wii matches a Wiimote on (lift from a real unit / wiibrew). Phase 1.
- **Q4 — Which Wiimote data report carries the guitar extension** (e.g. `0x34` = core buttons + 19 extension bytes vs `0x3d` = 21 extension bytes) and what the game expects. Phase 3.
- **Q5 — marvin↔fauxmote link** (UART bitmask mirror of the fretboard protocol vs USB CDC vs other). Deferred; revisit before Phase 4 integration.

---

  `0x057e`/`0x0306`, PIN = reversed BD_ADDR, guitar extension ID `00 00 A4 20 01 03`
  + 6-byte report). Captured in [`../SPEC.md`](../SPEC.md) §3.

  toolchain + hardware.
- Registered the subproject: journal added to `CLAUDE.md`, pointer row + repo-map
  entry added to root `SPEC.md`.

```c
#include "nvs_flash.h"
#include "esp_log.h"
#include "esp_bt.h"
#include "esp_bt_main.h"
#include "esp_gap_bt_api.h"

static const char *TAG = "fauxmote";

/* The Wii matches a Wiimote on this SDP device name. Phase 0 only advertises the
 * name and makes the radio discoverable; the HID device + the rest of the SDP
 * record (VID/PID/descriptor/Class-of-Device) and the PIN-request handling land
 * in Phase 1. See firmware/fauxmote/docs/journal.md. */
#define FAUXMOTE_BT_NAME "Nintendo RVL-CNT-01"

static void gap_cb(esp_bt_gap_cb_event_t event, esp_bt_gap_cb_param_t *param)
{
    switch (event) {
    case ESP_BT_GAP_AUTH_CMPL_EVT:
        ESP_LOGI(TAG, "auth complete, status=%d", param->auth_cmpl.stat);
        break;
    case ESP_BT_GAP_PIN_REQ_EVT:
        ESP_LOGI(TAG, "PIN requested (min_16_digit=%d)", param->pin_req.min_16_digit);
        break;
    default:
        ESP_LOGD(TAG, "gap event %d", event);
        break;
    }
}

void app_main(void)
{
    esp_err_t err = nvs_flash_init();
    if (err == ESP_ERR_NVS_NO_FREE_PAGES || err == ESP_ERR_NVS_NEW_VERSION_FOUND) {
        ESP_ERROR_CHECK(nvs_flash_erase());
        err = nvs_flash_init();
    }
    ESP_ERROR_CHECK(err);

    ESP_ERROR_CHECK(esp_bt_controller_mem_release(ESP_BT_MODE_BLE));
    esp_bt_controller_config_t cfg = BT_CONTROLLER_INIT_CONFIG_DEFAULT();
    ESP_ERROR_CHECK(esp_bt_controller_init(&cfg));
    ESP_ERROR_CHECK(esp_bt_controller_enable(ESP_BT_MODE_CLASSIC_BT));

    ESP_ERROR_CHECK(esp_bluedroid_init());
    ESP_ERROR_CHECK(esp_bluedroid_enable());

    ESP_ERROR_CHECK(esp_bt_gap_register_callback(gap_cb));
    ESP_ERROR_CHECK(esp_bt_gap_set_device_name(FAUXMOTE_BT_NAME));
    ESP_ERROR_CHECK(esp_bt_gap_set_scan_mode(ESP_BT_CONNECTABLE, ESP_BT_GENERAL_DISCOVERABLE));

    ESP_LOGI(TAG, "Phase 0: BR/EDR radio up, discoverable as \"%s\"", FAUXMOTE_BT_NAME);
}

```

# Adafruit ESP32 Feather V2 USB and LED Details

## USB-to-Serial Bridge Chip

The board uses a **CH9102F** USB-to-serial converter. According to the product page, "As of May 19, 2022 we have changed from using the SiLabs CP2102N to the CH9102F due to severe parts shortages and price increases." The CH9102F offers improved performance, with the board capable of "uploading at 921600 bps for speedy firmware loading."

## Connection Type

This board does **not** have native USB—it relies on the CH9102F serial bridge chip for USB communication.

## USB-C Connector and Auto-Reset

The Feather V2 features a "USB Type C port instead of Micro B" and includes "high speed upload with auto-reset and serial debug" capability.

## Status Indicators

The board includes multiple LED indicators: "Charge/User LEDs + status NeoPixel with pin-controlled power for low power usage." The NeoPixel's power is controllable via firmware, enabling the board to achieve ultra-low power consumption when the LED is disabled.

One correction to my driver advice: the current Feather V2 uses a **CH9102F** USB-serial chip (boards made before May 2022 used the SiLabs CP2102N). That changes which macOS driver you may need. Here's the full setup.

## Recommended: VS Code + the official Espressif extension

This is the easiest path on macOS — the extension installs ESP-IDF and the Xtensa toolchain for you.

**1. Base prerequisites**
```sh
xcode-select --install                       # git + compilers (if not already present)
brew install cmake ninja dfu-util ccache python   # IDF build deps
```

**2. Install the extension** — in VS Code, install **"Espressif IDF"** (publisher: Espressif Systems).

**3. Configure ESP-IDF** — Command Palette → **"ESP-IDF: Configure ESP-IDF Extension"** → **Express** → pick the latest **v5.x** release. It downloads ESP-IDF to `~/esp` and tools to `~/.espressif` (Apple Silicon is supported natively).

**4. Open the project** — open **`firmware/fauxmote/`** as the VS Code folder (not the repo root). The extension wants the folder containing the top-level [CMakeLists.txt](firmware/fauxmote/CMakeLists.txt) + [sdkconfig.defaults](firmware/fauxmote/sdkconfig.defaults) as the workspace root. (You can add it as a second folder to your existing repo workspace, but the IDF project should be the root the extension acts on.)

**5. Set the chip target** — Command Palette → **"ESP-IDF: Set Espressif Device Target"** → **esp32** (the Feather V2 is the *original* ESP32, not S3/C3). This is also what the README's `idf.py set-target esp32` does.

**6. USB-serial driver (the board-specific bit)**
- **CH9102F** (current boards, post-May-2022): if no `/dev/cu.wchusbserial*` appears when you plug in, install the WCH **CH34x/CH9102 macOS VCP driver** (from WCH's site). On recent macOS you'll then approve it in System Settings → Privacy & Security.
- **CP2102N** (older boards): the CP210x driver is built into macOS Big Sur+; the port shows as `/dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART` or `/dev/cu.usbserial-*` with no install.
- Use a **data-capable USB-C cable** (charge-only cables are a classic gotcha). The Feather V2 has auto-reset/auto-bootloader, so you don't need to hold BOOT to flash.

**7. Select port** — Command Palette → **"ESP-IDF: Select Port to Use"** → the `wchusbserial`/`SLAB` port.

**8. Build / flash / monitor** — use the status-bar icons (🔥 build, ⚡ flash, 🔌 monitor) or **"ESP-IDF: Build, Flash and Monitor"**. Success for Phase 0 = the serial log prints `Phase 0: BR/EDR radio up...` and the board shows up as `Nintendo RVL-CNT-01` in a phone/PC Bluetooth scan.

## Alternative: plain CLI (no extension)
```sh
mkdir -p ~/esp && cd ~/esp
git clone -b v5.4 --recursive https://github.com/espressif/esp-idf.git
cd esp-idf && ./install.sh esp32
. ./export.sh        # run this in each new shell (or alias it)
cd <repo>/firmware/fauxmote && idf.py set-target esp32 && idf.py build flash monitor
```

## Things worth knowing for this repo

- **Separate toolchain from marvin.** This is ESP-IDF/CMake — independent of marvin's MPLAB + OpenOCD/`arm-none-eabi-gdb` setup. The existing `.vscode/launch.json` debug configs don't apply here; the Espressif extension manages its own build/flash/debug.
- **JTAG debugging is optional and needs an external probe.** The original ESP32 has no built-in USB-JTAG (that's an S3/C3 feature), so source-level debugging would need an ESP-Prog or your FT2232-class adapter. You don't need it for Phase 0–1 — `idf.py monitor` (printf over serial) is enough to validate pairing.
- **If you ask *me* to flash/monitor, it'll fail in my command sandbox** — USB enumeration is blocked here (same constraint the marvin journal notes for OpenOCD). I'd need to run those with the sandbox disabled, or you run them. A plain `idf.py build` also won't work for me in-sandbox since installing IDF needs network beyond the Microchip allowlist.

Done. Created [firmware/fauxmote/.vscode/](firmware/fauxmote/.vscode/) with two committable files:

- **[extensions.json](firmware/fauxmote/.vscode/extensions.json)** — recommends the **Espressif IDF** extension + **C/C++ tools**, and marks **CMake Tools** as *unwanted* (it conflicts with the Espressif extension's own build management). Opening the folder will prompt to install these.
- **[settings.json](firmware/fauxmote/.vscode/settings.json)** — prefills the portable bits: target **`esp32`**, flash type **UART**, headers treated as C. The key trick is `"idf.saveScope": "global"` — when you run **"ESP-IDF: Configure ESP-IDF Extension"**, the extension writes the *machine-specific* paths (IDF location, tools, python, serial port) to your **user profile** instead of this file, so the committed `.vscode/` stays clean and portable across machines.

I deliberately left out `launch.json`/`c_cpp_properties.json`: those are machine-specific and need a JTAG probe config we don't have yet — the extension generates them locally if/when you add JTAG debugging. The existing [.gitignore](firmware/fauxmote/.gitignore) already covers `build/` and `sdkconfig`, so nothing machine-specific will leak.

So the flow is now: open `firmware/fauxmote/` in VS Code → accept the recommended extensions → run "Configure ESP-IDF Extension" (Express, v5.x) → the target's already set to esp32 → build/flash/monitor.
